newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Uncertain reception awaits returning Mir crew.
newsitem.headline: Uncertain reception awaits returning Mir crew.

text.p: Two Russian cosmonauts who are due to touch down on Earth this week after six months in space face an uncertain welcome after "some very dark times" on the stricken Mir orbital station.

Vasily Tsibliyev and Alexander Lazutkin blasted off on February 10 from the same desert in the former Soviet republic of Kazakhstan where their Soyuz craft will land on Thursday evening (around 1200 GMT).

Doctors and rescue teams, who will track Soyuz's progress by radio and in helicopters once a parachute opens to slow its plunge to Earth, will open the hatch and transfer the pair immediately to a waiting tent for routine medical checks.
They have been wearing specially-designed trousers to increase the pressure on their legs in preparation for the shock of gravity after six months of weightlessness.
But doctors will also be examining 43-year-old crew commander Tsibliyev for a heart problem he developed on Mir.
"The only thing I want to pray to God for is that Vasily comes back alive and healthy," his mother told Reuters last month in an interview at the meagre family home in Ukraine.

Tsibliyev and flight engineer Lazutkin, 39, can be sure of a joyous welcome from their families, who have had to make do with radio contact and the occasional television link-up with the cosmonauts during six worrying months.
But the official reception, expected to take place either at the military airport near Moscow to where they will be flown or the nearby Zvyozdny Gorodok (Star City), could be mixed.
"We have gone through some very dark times, but we are over them," Tsibliyev said recently.
Back in February, the two men could scarcely have guessed at the troubles awaiting them on Mir, whose various modules and solar panels make it look like a huge cosmic stick insect.
In less than a fortnight, a fire had broken out on the orbiting station. Tsibliyev, Lazutkin and the other four cosmonauts aboard had to don gas masks to avoid suffocation.
The two Russians who returned to Earth shortly afterwards were awarded medals for bravery for dealing with the fire, which was extinguished within minutes.
But officials have so far not mentioned any similar honours for Tsibliyev and Lazutkin.
On June 25, Mir suffered its worst accident ever when it collided with a cargo craft which Tsibliyev was manoeuvring, sending air rushing from Mir into the vacuum of outer space.

In their rush to seal the hole, they had to disconnect the cables to some of the solar panels, leaving it limping on half power. They have been unable to fix either that problem or trouble later with the 11-year-old station's oxygen supply.
Mission Control officials have been careful to shield the cosmonauts from bad news during their time in orbit so as not to put them through unnecessary stress.
Tsibliyev has not been told of his father-in-law's death and it is not clear whether he knows President Boris Yeltsin has said human error could have caused the June 25 crash.
The incident threw the entire future of Russia's lucrative space programme into doubt.
"Specialists have said that at first glance it was not due to technical failure and that apparently the human factor played a part, although it is impossible to say for sure," Yeltsin said on Friday.

A few weeks after the crash, Tsibliyev developed an irregular heart beat, which Mission Control said was due to stress. Just days later, someone pulled out a vital computer cable by mistake, cutting out the lights on the ship.

Their scheduled landing on Thursday will be just over six hours after they close the hatch on Mir having said goodbye to their American co-crew member Michael Foale and two Russian replacements who flew up last week.
If Tsibliyev's 64-year-old mother has anything to do with it, he at least won't be blasting off again.
